bst260projhelp

Overview

The final projects for BST260 will consist of pkgdown sites addressing data science concerns with public datasets. Objectives include

  • demonstrating understanding of how the R package and vignette concepts can be leveraged via pkgdown and GitHub pages to produce globally accessible web pages with your scientific goals and findings
  • illustrating methods of information transformation, such as extracting tables and figures from web sites or publications and repurposing them for communication and data analysis
  • consistently clarifying provenance of materials used in your project and future research, including efficient production of usable bibliographic references

Details

This repository provides documentation, functions, and example public documents to help with recurring tasks that arise when working with PDF reports or journal-article HTML.

  1. Table extraction – recovering structured tables from PDF pages, whether they’re laid out simply (one row per text line) or awkwardly (wrapped cells, centred columns, rotated pages), or from an HTML article’s own <table> elements.
  2. Bibliographic integrity – parsing a report’s own reference list, resolving its in-text citations against that list, and exporting the result as BibTeX or CSL-JSON, so that a table of cited studies (or a curated list of cited systems/datasets) can be checked rather than taken on faith.

Table extraction comes in two flavors, matched to how awkward a table’s layout is:

  • Simple layouts (pdf_read_count_pct_table(), pdf_read_wide_wrapped_table() and friends) work line-by-line off pdftools::pdf_text(), which is enough when each table row is already one clean line of text.
  • Word-geometry extraction (pdf_read_table() and friends) is for tables where that breaks down – wrapped cells, centred rather than left-aligned headers, or records with no blank line between them. Instead of plain text, it reads pdftools::pdf_data(), which gives the x/y position of every individual word on the page. From those coordinates it reconstructs the table itself: clustering words into text lines by vertical position, then into columns by their horizontal position (an edge or centre you supply), then grouping lines back into records. “Word-geometry” just names this: the table structure is recovered from where words sit on the page, not from line breaks in the extracted text.

A third mode works from HTML instead of PDF: rvest-based scraping of a PMC journal-article page, where both the tables and the reference list are already machine-structured (a real <table> element; a reference list where every in-text citation marker is itself a link straight to its entry), so the work is reading the right elements correctly rather than reconstructing structure from plain text or page geometry.

Three worked examples are bundled as package data and vignettes:

  • a RAND report on gun policy research (vignette("gun-legislation")), with a RAND-style, per-chapter, author-year bibliography;
  • a CDC waterborne disease surveillance report (vignette("waterborne-disease")), with a numbered (Vancouver-style) bibliography;
  • a PMC journal article on stroke mortality (vignette("html-scraping")), with its own pre-structured, numbered reference list.

Installation 

# install.packages("devtools") 
devtools::install_github("vjcitn/bst260projhelp", build_vignettes = TRUE)

Origin

The functions in R/ were generalized from exploratory scripts written against these specific documents; those original scripts (and the source PDFs/HTML) are kept in data-raw/ for reference. See data-raw/gunleg/README.txt and data-raw/waterborne/README.txt for the project prompts the PDF-extraction functions were written to answer; the HTML-scraping functions were generalized directly from the PMC article cached at data-raw/htmlscrape/.
